success_patterns: In every success the clue was a near-paraphrase of a sentence repeated across several independent passages (polonium 'named in honor of her native land', Bastille 'eighteen years', Israel 'four major land regions'). The agent took the entity that recurs next to the clue's rarest details and matched the slot noun ('this prison', 'this element', 'this country').
The answers were bare short names with no type word or clue words ('Polka', 'Polonium', 'Sahara', 'Israel', 'Ritalin'). The category noun in the clue was dropped.
When the passages listed several valid names for the same thing (Ritalin, Concerta, Metadate as trade names), the agent chose the best-known, most-repeated one, which was also the first-listed one.

When the clue gave an alias or fictional stand-in for a real original ('parodied this detective as Hemlock Jones'), the agent answered the original that passages call the target of the 'parody of ...'. It did not answer the alias, the author or the clue's own anchors.

For a colon or quoted-pun clue ('A comedienne:"Ball of Fire"'), the agent combined the category before the colon with the quoted word and its own knowledge. The answer fit both halves, so it did not need a verbatim archive hit.

patch.reasoning: The skill already covers most of what worked: Rule 3 (clue repeated in the passages), Rule 4 (bare core answer), and the colon and quoted-pun rules. Two gaps remain. First, there is no tie-breaker when several equally valid names fit, such as brand or trade names and aliases; the agent resolved this by picking the most repeated, best-known one. Second, there is no rule for 'parody / imitation / modeled-on' alias clues, where the answer is the original that the clue's alias stands in for. Both fixes are short single bullets inserted next to related rules, to avoid more bloat.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - Several equally valid names for the same thing (trade or brand names, aliases, synonyms, 'also called'): choose the one the passages repeat most and present as the standard or best-known example, usually the one listed first ('known by this trade name' -> the headline brand, not a minor variant or extended-release label). Do not pick a rarer name just because it appears once beside the clue's words.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content: - Parody / imitation / alias clues ('a tale parodied this detective as Hemlock Jones', 'modeled on this man', 'a spoof of this'): the alias or spoof name in the clue and the author who wrote it are anchors. The answer is the ORIGINAL that passages call the target ('a parody of Sherlock Holmes'), in its standard name.
